title: The Two Numbers That Appear Only Once

concept.title: XOR everything, then split the numbers by a bit in which the two answers differ
body: In a list every value appears **twice**, except **two different values** that appear **once**. Find those two. For `1 2 1 3 2 5` the answers are 3 and 5. If there were only one such value, XOR-ing all numbers would give it, since `x ^ x = 0`. Here the XOR gives `x = p ^ q`, the XOR of the two unknown values, which is **not zero** because `p` and `q` are different.

The number `x = p ^ q` has a bit equal to 1 exactly where `p` and `q` **differ**. Take any such bit, for example the lowest one: `low = x & -x` (this trick keeps only the lowest set bit). Now split all the numbers into two groups by this bit: the numbers that **have** the bit and the numbers that **do not**. `p` and `q` fall into **different groups**, and every pair of equal numbers falls into the **same** group.

body.code:
x = 0
for v in a: x ^= v                 # x = p ^ q
low = x & -x                       # a bit where p and q differ
p = q = 0
for v in a:
    if v & low: p ^= v             # one group: the pairs cancel, p remains
    else:       q ^= v             # the other group: q remains
print(min(p, q), max(p, q))

body: In each group the equal pairs cancel by XOR, and exactly one of the unknown values is left, so the two XORs are the two answers. The program makes two passes and uses O(1) memory: O(n) time. The expression `x & -x` works because `-x` is `~x + 1`, which flips all the bits above the lowest set bit and keeps that bit.

statement: A list has `n` numbers. Every value appears exactly twice except two different values, each of which appears exactly once. Print these two values in increasing order.
inputFormat: The first line has `n`: the number of values.
The second line has `n` numbers. Every value appears exactly twice except two different values, which appear once each.
outputFormat: Print the two values separated by a space, the smaller first.
hints: The XOR of the whole list is p ^ q.
The lowest set bit of p ^ q is a bit where p and q differ.
XOR the numbers of each group (with and without that bit) separately.

explanation: The XOR of all numbers equals p ^ q; its lowest set bit separates p from q, and XOR-ing the two groups of numbers separately leaves p in one group and q in the other.

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))

x = 0
for v in a:
    x ^= v
low = x & -x
p = q = 0
for v in a:
    if v & low:
        p ^= v
    else:
        q ^= v
print(min(p, q), max(p, q))
